source_text: Ergo contra hanc nitens ire sententiam pariter fieri asserat, quod pariter ne fieret imperatum est. Facilius quippe lex Dei negari quam emendari potest et, licet sit profana negatio, profanior tamen absurdiorque correctio est. Si enim de duobus eius decretis unum venereris, alterum exsecreris, ingratus ab eius parte, quod suscipis, et illi cogeris oboedire, quod respuis, quoniam unius quod tibi carum est dignitate, etiam id, quod adversabare, defenditur atque absurdissime ea se quisquam credit praecepta venerari, quorum partem audet incessere. Unde consequentius potest negari lex universa quam corrigi; nemo autem eam corrigere nisi impius quisque tentabit; a religiosis ergo et prudentibus tota suscipitur, tota laudatur. Nec sane quemquam moveat, quod ritum sacrificiorum veterum Novi Testamenti videat aetate cessasse. Non est una ratio virtutum et hostiarum: alia est praeceptorum perennitas, alia sacrificiorum temporalitas. Veniente tamen Christo, qui hostiis figurabatur antiquis, impleta sunt, non condemnata, quae fuerant instituta; neque enim suis temporibus praedicuntur exercita, sed succedente perfectione, quae promissa officiis eorum fuerant, quieverunt.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore straining to go against this sentence let him assert that that equally happens which was equally commanded not to happen. For the law of God can more easily be denied than emended, and although denial is profane, correction is nevertheless more profane and more absurd. For if of its two decrees you venerate one and execrate the other, ungrateful from the part you take up, you are also forced to obey that which you spit out, since by the dignity of the one which is dear to you even that which you were opposing is defended, and most absurdly anyone believes he venerates those precepts whose part he dares to attack. Whence more consequently the whole law can be denied than corrected; but no one except an impious person will attempt to correct it; by the religious and prudent therefore it is taken up whole, praised whole. Nor indeed should it move anyone that he sees the rite of the old sacrifices has ceased in the age of the New Testament. There is not one account of virtues and of victims: one thing is the perenniality of precepts, another the temporality of sacrifices. Yet with Christ coming, who was figured by the ancient victims, those things which had been instituted were fulfilled, not condemned; for they are not denounced as having been exercised in their own times, but with perfection succeeding, which had been promised to their offices, they came to rest.

pass_b_english: Anyone determined to oppose this pronouncement, then, should assert that both things happen, when both were equally forbidden. For it is easier to reject God’s law than to correct it. Rejection is irreverent, but correction is still more irreverent and absurd. If you honor one of its two decrees and detest the other, the part you accept will force you, against your will, to obey the part you reject. The dignity of the one you value also defends the one you opposed. It is completely absurd to imagine you honor commands when you dare attack part of them. Thus rejecting the whole law is more consistent than correcting it. Yet only an impious person will attempt to correct it; devout and sensible people accept and praise it in its entirety.

No one should be troubled here by seeing that the old sacrificial rites ceased in the age of the New Testament. Virtues and sacrificial victims are not governed by the same principle: commands are enduring; sacrifices are temporary. Yet when Christ came, whom the ancient sacrifices foreshadowed, what had been established was fulfilled, not condemned. Those observances are not denounced as having been practiced in their proper times; they came to rest when the perfection promised through their service arrived (Matthew 5:17) (Hebrews 10:1).
